Summary  
This article recounts how insider trading on the play-money prediction-market platform Manifold publicly revealed—in advance—the planned publication date of the “CAIS AI risk” extinction-warning statement signed by leading AI CEOs.  The narrative links the top-level existential risk from advanced AI to intermediate concerns about information-security failures, insider trading dynamics, and platform-governance gaps that reduced the intended impact of an important public-awareness intervention.  It implicitly and explicitly discusses a set of mitigations: private (non-public) markets, clearer deletion/restriction policies, question-design guidelines, insider-trading detection, and lower-visibility settings.

EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[86]  
• The source gives rich causal explanations that can be cleanly mapped onto one connected fabric; all nodes reference explicit sections.  
• Node names follow the required granularity and should merge well across datasets.  
• Interventions use action-verb naming and are mapped to lifecycle and maturity with justification.  
Possible prompt improvement: make explicit whether narrative-style sources without formal headers should let the extractor create synthetic section-title references when none exist.

Inference strategy justification  
The paper proposes most interventions explicitly (private groups, deletion policy, better question design, limiting visibility).  Insider-trading detection is moderately inferred as the natural technical response to the documented distortion and leak; confidence is marked low (1) and the edge notes inference.

Extraction completeness explanation  
Fifteen interconnected nodes capture every distinct risk→mechanism→finding→intervention step the article presents, with no orphan nodes or direct risk-to-intervention edges.  All proposed mitigations are represented and traceable to the narrative.

Key limitations  
• The article is anecdotal; evidence strengths are necessarily low–medium.  
• Some causal directions (e.g., transparency ethos → policy gap) are qualitative; confidence reflects that.  
• Interventions lie mostly at policy/community levels, so lifecycle stages are approximate.
